title: Single Responsibility Principle
summary: A class should answer to one actor, not do literally one thing — each reason to change belongs to its own collaborator.
signals: one class (often named `*Service` or `*Manager`) that validates a business rule, formats a message, and writes a log in the same method
a bug fix to wording (an email subject, a log format) that also touches the class owning an unrelated business rule
a single test asserting three unrelated outcomes — a status change, a message body, and a log line — because they can't be exercised apart
a change requested by one stakeholder (support, legal, ops) that forces edits in code another stakeholder (product) also depends on

roles.OrderService: before: one class doing all three jobs — the cancellation rule, the email wording, and the audit format
roles.CancelOrder: after: high-level policy that owns only the cancellation rule
roles.OrderNotifier: after: collaborator that owns the email wording
roles.AuditLog: after: collaborator that owns the audit entry format

stages.title: Three reasons to change
stages.idea: OrderService cancels the order, formats the customer email, and writes the audit log in one class and one method.

stages.title: One reason each
stages.idea: CancelOrder owns only the cancellation rule; OrderNotifier and AuditLog each own one remaining concern and are tested alone.

checks: "A class should do one thing" is a common but misleading phrasing of SRP. What should replace "thing", and why does that fix the phrasing?
In the before version of OrderService, name the three actors who could each ask for an independent change, and what each would ask for.
Why does extracting OrderNotifier reduce how many tests you re-run when marketing changes the email wording, even though the total number of tests goes up?
When would splitting the audit-log call into its own class be over-engineering rather than an application of SRP?
